semantics: Launch set of the Evidence-Graded Claims Library (portfolio plan 3.4), free public summaries only; gated depth waits for membership infrastructure. Two axes: grade_strength (strong | moderate | limited | insufficient | contradicted) describes the evidence for the claim as parents state it; grade_consensus (consensus | majority | divided | fringe) describes where the field sits. The claims grader enforces: every claim fully fielded, at least two sources each, hedging language present wherever strength is limited or insufficient, no overclaim vocabulary above the grade, reading level, and enum validity. Per the production pipeline, the model proposes and Matthew disposes: grades carry drafted status until his review flips it (keel/REVIEW.md).

claims.claim_text: Sleep training will damage my baby's attachment to me.
claims.verdict_label: The studies that looked for attachment harm did not find it.
claims.summary_public: This is one of the most anxiety-producing claims in parenting, so it matters that it has actually been tested. Randomized trials of behavioral sleep interventions, including graduated extinction, measured infant stress, parent-child attachment, and child emotional and behavioral outcomes, and did not find harm. The longest follow-up tracked families for five years and found no differences in attachment security, behavior, or the parent-child relationship between sleep-trained children and controls. Two honest caveats belong here. First, these studies mostly involve infants over six months, so they say little about sleep training a very young baby. Second, absence of detected harm across a handful of trials is not the same as proof of total safety for every method at every age; the trials used gentler, parent-present variants more often than strict versions. What the evidence contradicts is the specific, frightening claim that responding less at night damages the bond of a securely attached child. It does not tell any family that they must sleep train; that remains a values call, and children whose parents choose either path do fine.

sources.citation: Gradisar M, Jackson K, Spurrier NJ, et al. Behavioral interventions for infant sleep problems: a randomized controlled trial. Pediatrics. 2016;137(6):e20151486.
sources.role: RCT including cortisol and attachment measures

sources.citation: Price AM, Wake M, Ukoumunne OC, Hiscock H. Five-year follow-up of harms and benefits of behavioral infant sleep intervention. Pediatrics. 2012;130(4):643-651.
sources.role: Longest randomized follow-up; no attachment or behavior differences at age 6

sources.citation: Mindell JA, Kuhn B, Lewin DS, Meltzer LJ, Sadeh A. Behavioral treatment of bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children. Sleep. 2006;29(10):1263-1276.
sources.role: Task-force review of the behavioral-intervention literature

claims.claim_text: Hearing two languages will confuse my baby and delay their speech.
claims.verdict_label: Bilingual children hit language milestones on schedule when you count both languages.
claims.summary_public: The confusion myth is one of the clearest cases in this library. The developmental science field is unusually united here. Children exposed to two languages from birth babble on time, say first words on time, and combine words on time. The catch is how you count: their vocabulary lives across both languages, so measuring one language against monolingual norms undercounts them. Code-mixing, using both languages in one sentence, is not confusion. Bilingual adults mix in systematic, grammatical ways, and bilingual children's mixing follows the same patterns. The practical harm of this myth is specific and documented. Families are told to drop a home language to help speech, which sacrifices a real relationship asset for no developmental gain. And clinicians sometimes delay evaluating a bilingual child who genuinely needs help, because lateness gets misattributed to bilingualism. The red lines for a language conversation with your pediatrician are the same for bilingual children as for anyone, counted across all languages.

sources.citation: Byers-Heinlein K, Lew-Williams C. Bilingualism in the early years: what the science says. LEARNing Landscapes. 2013;7(1):95-112.
sources.role: Accessible research review of early bilingual development

sources.citation: Hoff E, Core C. What clinicians need to know about bilingual development. Seminars in Speech and Language. 2015;36(2):89-99.
sources.role: Clinical guidance: total-vocabulary counting, referral timing

claims.claim_text: A baby walker will help my baby learn to walk sooner.
claims.verdict_label: Walkers don't speed walking, and the injury record is bad enough that the AAP wants them banned.
claims.summary_public: This one earns the library's rarest combination: the product does not deliver its named benefit, and it carries a documented injury cost. Controlled research found that infants who used walkers sat, crawled, and walked no earlier than infants who did not. Some studies measured slightly later motor milestones and lower motor scores during the walker months. The likely reason is simple: time in the device replaces the floor time where those skills are actually built. Meanwhile, walkers give pre-walking babies speed and reach they cannot control. Thousands of emergency-room visits, with stair falls as the signature injury, led the American Academy of Pediatrics to call for a ban on manufacture and sale. Canada did ban them in 2004. A stationary activity center delivers the upright entertainment without the wheels. The floor remains the best walking teacher ever devised. If a walker is already in your house, enjoy the floor more, and keep the walker far from any stairs.

sources.citation: Siegel AC, Burton RV. Effects of baby walkers on motor and mental development in human infants. Journal of Developmental & Behavioral Pediatrics. 1999;20(5):355-361.
sources.role: Controlled comparison of walker and non-walker infants

sources.citation: American Academy of Pediatrics, Committee on Injury and Poison Prevention. Injuries associated with infant walkers. Pediatrics. 2001;108(3):790-792.
sources.role: Injury data and the AAP's ban recommendation

claims.claim_text: Tummy time actually matters for my baby's development.
claims.verdict_label: Yes: prone play time is linked to better motor development, and short frequent sessions count.
claims.summary_public: Tummy time is one of the few pieces of standard baby advice with a systematic review behind it. Across 16 studies of over 4,000 infants, more awake prone time was associated with better gross motor development and less flattening of the back of the head, with some evidence for benefits to early rolling and crawling. The honest grading note: most of the underlying studies are observational, so the strength here is moderate rather than strong; babies who get more floor time may differ from babies who don't in other ways too. But the mechanism is plain, the direction is consistent, and the practice costs nothing. What the evidence does not support is tummy-time guilt. The benefit comes from accumulated awake prone play, and short, frequent, tolerable sessions, including tummy-on-your-chest time, add up to the same place as long formal ones. A baby who protests three minutes in is not falling behind; they're asking you to make it more interesting, which is a solvable problem.

sources.citation: Hewitt L, Kerr E, Stanley RM, Okely AD. Tummy time and infant health outcomes: a systematic review. Pediatrics. 2020;145(6):e20192168.
sources.role: Systematic review, 16 studies

sources.citation: American Academy of Pediatrics. Safe sleep and skull shaping guidance: back to sleep, tummy to play.
sources.role: The supervised-and-awake framing every session should follow

claims.claim_text: Screen time is harming my toddler's language development.
claims.verdict_label: Heavy, passive, background screen use is linked to less language input; the dose and the type matter more than the screen.
claims.summary_public: The screen-time literature rewards precision, because the honest answer depends on what is actually happening. Large studies do find that heavier screen exposure in the first years is associated with lower scores on developmental and language screens. The mechanism is well documented. Screens tend to displace the back-and-forth talk that builds language, and background TV measurably reduces both the quantity and the quality of parent speech. Young toddlers also learn much less from video than from a live person, the well-replicated video-deficit effect. What the same literature does not support is panic over moderate, co-viewed use. Video chat behaves more like conversation than like TV, and an adult watching alongside and talking about the content changes the equation. These are also mostly associations; families with heavy screen use differ in many other ways, which is why the strength grade is moderate. The practical read: protect daily stretches of screen-free back-and-forth, cut background TV first, and worry less about the occasional co-watched show.

sources.citation: Madigan S, Browne D, Racine N, Mori C, Tough S. Association between screen time and children's performance on a developmental screening test. JAMA Pediatrics. 2019;173(3):244-250.
sources.role: Longitudinal association between screen hours and developmental screening scores

sources.citation: Anderson DR, Pempek TA. Television and very young children. American Behavioral Scientist. 2005;48(5):505-522.
sources.role: Video-deficit effect and background-TV displacement research

claims.claim_text: Pacifier use will delay my child's speech.
claims.verdict_label: The feared speech link is not well supported; the real documented tradeoffs are ear infections and dental effects with prolonged use.
claims.summary_public: For ordinary pacifier use in the first couple of years, the evidence for speech harm is weak. The studies are few, small, and mixed. No solid body of research shows that typical pacifier use delays speech or language development. The honest grade is simply that we do not have enough evidence, and the loud warnings outrun the data. What the literature does document is different and worth knowing. Pacifier use is associated with more ear infections. Heavy use that continues past the toddler years is associated with dental changes. There is also a protective association with SIDS when a pacifier is offered at sleep in the early months, which is why sleep guidance often favors them early on. The pragmatic read fits this evidence. A pacifier in the first year or two is not a speech risk worth losing sleep over. A mouth that is always occupied during awake, chatty hours gets less talking practice, for obvious mechanical reasons. And weaning somewhere in the second or third year keeps you clear of the tradeoffs that are actually documented.

sources.citation: Sexton S, Natale R. Risks and benefits of pacifiers. American Family Physician. 2009;79(8):681-685.
sources.role: Clinical review of documented benefits and harms

sources.citation: Nelson AM. A comprehensive review of evidence and current recommendations related to pacifier usage. Journal of Pediatric Nursing. 2012;27(6):690-699.
sources.role: Evidence review across speech, dental, ear-infection, and SIDS outcomes

claims.claim_text: Talking to my baby, even before they can respond, builds their language.
claims.verdict_label: Yes, and the back-and-forth matters even more than the word count.
claims.summary_public: This is the best-supported claim in early language science, with one important modern refinement. Decades of research link the amount of speech directed at a child to vocabulary growth, and the famous '30 million word gap' figure made that finding a headline; the specific number comes from a small 1990s sample and has been fairly criticized. But the refined finding is stronger, not weaker: longitudinal work following children's real language environments found that conversational turns, the back-and-forth exchanges where an adult responds to a child and waits, predict language outcomes and even language-related brain activity better than raw word counts do, and independent of family income. The practical translation is genuinely freeing. You do not need to monologue all day or perform enrichment. You need to respond: treat your baby's sounds, gestures, and eventually words as conversational serves, return them, and wait for the next one. Narration helps; responsiveness does the heavy lifting. Every tool on this site that touches language is built on that mechanism.

sources.citation: Gilkerson J, Richards JA, Warren SF, et al. Language experience in the second year of life and language outcomes in late childhood. Pediatrics. 2018;142(4):e20174276.
sources.role: Longitudinal: early conversational turns predict outcomes a decade later

sources.citation: Romeo RR, Leonard JA, Robinson ST, et al. Beyond the 30-million-word gap: children's conversational exposure is associated with language-related brain function. Psychological Science. 2018;29(5):700-710.
sources.role: Conversational turns and Broca's-area activation, independent of SES

claims.verdict_label: Teething can nudge temperature up slightly; it does not cause true fever.
claims.summary_public: A meta-analysis across studies of primary tooth eruption settled this about as cleanly as pediatric questions get. Teething is genuinely associated with gum irritation, drooling, fussiness, and a slight rise in temperature on eruption days. It is not associated with fever in the clinical sense, meaning 38C (100.4F) or above. Why this matters more than it seems: teething happens on and off for two years, which makes it an available explanation for almost any symptom. The documented danger is attribution error. A baby with a real fever who is assumed to be 'just teething' is a baby whose actual illness, often an ear infection or a virus, is being explained away by a coincidence of timing. The evidence-based rule is worth keeping. Fussiness, gnawing, and drool with a barely-elevated temperature fits teething. An actual fever means treat the child as sick, and call your pediatrician if you would have called for that fever anyway, teeth or no teeth.

sources.citation: Massignan C, Cardoso M, Porporatti AL, et al. Signs and symptoms of primary tooth eruption: a meta-analysis. Pediatrics. 2016;137(3):e20153501.
sources.role: Meta-analysis: eruption symptoms real, true fever not among them

sources.citation: Markman L. Teething: facts and fiction. Pediatrics in Review. 2009;30(8):e59-e64.
sources.role: Clinical review of the attribution-error problem

claims.claim_text: Baby-led weaning is better than spoon-feeding purées.
claims.verdict_label: A fine approach, not a superior one; the trial evidence shows mostly equivalence.
claims.summary_public: Baby-led weaning arrived with big claims: better self-regulation, less picky eating, lower obesity risk. When the approach finally got a randomized trial, the BLISS study, the headline results were mostly equivalence. There was no significant difference in weight or overweight risk at 12 and 24 months compared with traditional spoon-feeding. Reassuringly, there was also no increase in choking events when families got guidance on safe food shapes and sizes. Evidence for the softer claims, less pickiness and better appetite regulation, remains limited and mixed. It comes mainly from parent-report and observational work, where families who choose baby-led weaning differ in many other ways. So the honest grade is limited: not contradicted, not established, and with the safety question reasonably addressed under proper guidance on iron-rich foods and choking-aware preparation. The practical translation is unusually low-stakes. Both roads lead to a toddler who eats table food. Pick the one that fits your household, mix them freely, and spend the reclaimed worry elsewhere.

sources.citation: Taylor RW, Williams SM, Fangupo LJ, et al. Effect of a baby-led approach to complementary feeding on infant growth and overweight: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA Pediatrics. 2017;171(9):838-846.
sources.role: The BLISS randomized trial: growth equivalence

sources.citation: Brown A, Jones SW, Rowan H. Baby-led weaning: the evidence to date. Current Nutrition Reports. 2017;6(2):148-156.
sources.role: Review of the observational literature and its limits

claims.claim_text: Reading to my toddler actually changes their language development.
claims.verdict_label: Yes, and reading interactively, with questions and pauses, roughly doubles the effect.
claims.summary_public: Shared book reading is one of the most-studied parent behaviors in developmental science, and it holds up. Children who are read to more develop larger vocabularies and stronger early literacy skills. The finding with real practical teeth is about how you read. In the original dialogic reading experiments, parents were taught to turn reading into a conversation: ask open questions, follow the child's answers, expand them, and let the child tell parts of the story. Children in those conditions showed measurably larger expressive-language gains than children who were simply read to, within weeks. A later meta-analysis confirmed the added value of the interactive style, strongest for two- and three-year-olds. The mechanism is the same back-and-forth engine documented across this library. A book is simply the best conversation-holder ever invented, because the pictures pin joint attention in one place. And reading the same book 400 times, a toddler specialty, is a feature. Familiarity is what frees them to do the talking.

sources.citation: Whitehurst GJ, Falco FL, Lonigan CJ, et al. Accelerating language development through picture book reading. Developmental Psychology. 1988;24(4):552-559.
sources.role: The original dialogic reading experiment

sources.citation: Mol SE, Bus AG, de Jong MT, Smeets DJH. Added value of dialogic parent-child book readings: a meta-analysis. Early Education and Development. 2008;19(1):7-26.
sources.role: Meta-analysis of the interactive-reading effect
